items.title: Patagonia's owner gave the company to the planet
items.claim: In September 2022, Yvon Chouinard announced he was transferring ownership of Patagonia. What was the structure?

options.text: An IPO on the New York Stock Exchange
All voting stock to the Patagonia Purpose Trust (climate-aligned governance); all non-voting stock (98%) to the Holdfast Collective, with future profits funding environmental causes
A sale to a private equity buyer

items.reveal:
Chouinard, his wife Malinda and their two children transferred Patagonia (valued around $3bn) using two vehicles: the Purpose Trust holds voting control to ensure mission alignment; the Holdfast Collective (a 501(c)(4) nonprofit) holds economic ownership and receives roughly $100m of annual profits to fund environmental work.

The structure required the family to pay $17.5m in gift tax. The company is a B Corp (certified since 2011) — the legal structure goes much further than B Corp certification alone.

B Lab's B Corp movement, launched in 2006, certifies firms meeting social and environmental performance standards.
items.why: Corporate ownership structures shape objectives. A trust-owned firm doesn't have to maximise shareholder returns — because its 'shareholders' are not the same as a public company's.

items.title: Taylor's piece rate was an incentive, not a wage
items.claim: F.W. Taylor at Bethlehem Steel in the 1890s introduced piece-rate pay. What was the central design feature?

options.text: All workers received the same base pay regardless of output
Workers were paid per unit produced, with the 'scientific' target set so only those following Taylor's prescribed method could earn the bonus
Piece rates were determined by union negotiation

items.reveal_title: Pay per piece, conditional on method
items.reveal:
Taylor's pig-iron handling experiments at Bethlehem Steel (1898-99) raised loading from 12.5 to 47 tons per worker per day. Workers earning the bonus received about 60% more pay; the firm got 280% more output per worker.

Unions opposed Taylorism fiercely — 1911 US Congressional hearings investigated 'speed-up' abuses. Modern piece rates persist in garment factories, gig economy (Uber surge pricing as a variant) and sales commissions.
items.why: Piece rates align effort with output but can erode quality, safety and worker autonomy. The same design principle reappears in 'pay for performance' compensation a century later.

items.title: Kodak invented the digital camera in 1975
items.claim: Steven Sasson, a Kodak engineer, built the first digital camera prototype in 1975. What happened to it?

options.text: Kodak rushed it to market and dominated the digital camera industry
Kodak management, worried about cannibalising film sales, suppressed the project; the company filed for bankruptcy in 2012 having failed the digital transition
It was stolen by a competitor before it could be developed

items.reveal:
Sasson's prototype was a 3.6 kg device using a CCD sensor and a cassette tape, taking 23 seconds to capture a 0.01 megapixel black-and-white image. He filed a patent in 1978.

Kodak's response, as Sasson later recalled, was 'that's cute, but don't tell anyone about it.' Film and processing had 60-70% gross margins. Kodak did launch digital products from the 1990s but couldn't restructure around a business model with lower margins.

The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January 2012.
items.why: Owning the future technology isn't enough — you have to be willing to destroy your current revenue. Few large organisations can.
